topics.title: Functions are objects you can pass around

kcs.statement: In Python a function is an object: it can be assigned to a name, stored in a container, passed as an argument and returned from another function.
Writing f refers to the function object itself; writing f() calls it and evaluates to its return value.

topics.title: Closures: inner functions that remember

kcs.statement: A nested function that references a variable of its enclosing function keeps access to that variable after the outer function returns; this is a closure.
Closures capture variables, not values: functions created in a loop over i all see i's final value unless the current value is bound, for example as a default argument.
Assigning to an enclosing function's variable inside a nested function requires a nonlocal declaration; without it the name is local, and reading it before assignment raises UnboundLocalError.

requires.reason: A closure is returned as a function object, so returning functions must already be familiar.

topics.title: What a decorator is

kcs.statement: A decorator is a callable that takes a function (or class) and returns an object that is then bound to the original name.
A decorator may return the original function unchanged, after registering or annotating it, or a different callable that wraps it.

serves.reason: Desugaring needs the definition of what a decorator receives and returns.

requires.reason: A decorator is defined as a function that takes and returns function objects.

topics.title: @ syntax desugars to func = dec(func)

kcs.statement: Writing @dec above def f(): ... is equivalent to defining f and then executing f = dec(f), except the undecorated function is never bound to the name f.
The expression after @ is evaluated once, when the def statement executes and before the function object is created; since Python 3.9 (PEP 614) it may be any expression.

serves.reason: Desugaring @ into an explicit assignment is the core of o1.

requires.reason: The desugaring applies a decorator, which must already be defined.

topics.title: Writing a wrapper that works for any signature

kcs.statement: A typical decorator defines an inner wrapper that runs extra code, calls the original function captured in its closure, and is returned in its place.
A wrapper defined as wrapper(*args, **kwargs) that calls func(*args, **kwargs) works for any signature of the decorated function.
A wrapper must return the result of calling the original function; omitting the return makes every decorated call return None.

serves.reason: Writing a signature-agnostic wrapper is the observable product of o2.

requires.reason: The wrapper reaches the original function through a closure.
The wrapper is the replacement a decorator returns.

topics.title: When decorator code runs: definition vs call

kcs.statement: A decorator's own body runs once, when the def statement executes (usually at import time), not each time the decorated function is called.
Code inside the returned wrapper runs on every call of the decorated name; code outside the wrapper runs only at decoration time.

serves.reason: Predicting printed output and call order depends on separating decoration time from call time.
Explaining when a registry or class decorator runs needs this distinction.

requires.reason: Decoration time is when the desugared assignment executes.
Call-time code lives in the wrapper.

topics.title: Preserving metadata with functools.wraps

kcs.statement: Without functools.wraps, the decorated name's __name__ and __doc__ are those of the wrapper, not of the original function.
Applying @functools.wraps(func) to the wrapper copies __module__, __name__, __qualname__, __doc__ and __annotations__ from func and merges func's __dict__ into the wrapper's.
functools.wraps sets wrapper.__wrapped__ to func, so inspect.signature reports the original signature and the undecorated function stays reachable.

serves.reason: o2 requires keeping __name__ and __doc__, which is exactly what wraps does.

requires.reason: wraps is applied to a wrapper function.

topics.title: Decorators with arguments: decorator factories

kcs.statement: A decorator with arguments is a factory: @dec(args) first calls dec(args), which must return the actual decorator that then receives the function.
@retry(times=3) above def f is equivalent to f = retry(times=3)(f).
The factory's arguments are captured in a closure, so the wrapper can read them on every call.
Writing @retry without parentheses when retry is a factory passes the function as the factory's first argument, so the name becomes bound to the inner decorator instead of a wrapper.

serves.reason: The three-level factory structure is the skeleton of @retry(times=3).
o1 requires desugaring decorators with arguments.

requires.reason: The factory desugaring extends func = dec(func).
The innermost level of a factory is a wrapper.

topics.title: Building @retry(times=3): loops, except and re-raise

kcs.statement: A retry wrapper loops over its attempts, returns func(*args, **kwargs) immediately on the first success, and catches only the designated exception types in its except clause.
On the final failed attempt the wrapper re-raises with a bare raise inside the except block, which propagates the original exception and traceback instead of falling through and returning None.
times counts total attempts, not extra retries; the factory should raise ValueError for times < 1 when it is called, because a zero-attempt loop never calls func and silently returns None.

serves.reason: Implementing a correct @retry(times=3) is o3's observable product and needs this control flow.

requires.reason: retry is a factory whose times argument lives in the closure.

topics.title: Stacking decorators and the order they apply

kcs.statement: Stacked decorators apply bottom-up: @a above @b above def f is equivalent to f = a(b(f)).

The decorator expressions of a stack are evaluated top-down before the function object is created, then applied bottom-up: @make('a') above @make('b') above def f is d_a = make('a'); d_b = make('b'); define f; f = d_a(d_b(f)).
When a stacked function is called, the top decorator's pre-call code runs first and its post-call code runs last, like nested layers.
Reordering stacked decorators can change behaviour: with @cache above @timer, cache hits never reach the timer, so they print no timing.

serves.reason: o1 explicitly includes stacked decorators, stacked factories and their printed order.

requires.reason: Stacking is repeated application of the desugaring.
Call order is about nested wrappers' pre- and post-call code.
The evaluate-top-down KC is checked on stacked factory calls that print when evaluated.

topics.title: functools.partial: freezing arguments

kcs.statement: functools.partial(func, *args, **kw) returns a callable that calls func with the frozen positional arguments first, followed by those given at call time, and with the frozen keywords merged in.
A partial object exposes .func, .args and .keywords, and keyword arguments given at call time override frozen keywords.

topics.title: Decorators usable as @dec and @dec(...)

kcs.statement: A decorator usable as both @dec and @dec(...) checks its first positional argument: if it is the function it decorates directly; if it is None it returns a decorator.
Making the options keyword-only, as in def dec(func=None, *, times=3), prevents a positional option from being mistaken for the function.
In the @dec(...) branch, returning functools.partial(dec, times=times) gives a callable that later receives the function as func.

serves.reason: o3 explicitly asks for a decorator usable both as @dec and @dec(...).

topics.title: Registration decorators and plugin registries

kcs.statement: A registration decorator adds the function to a registry, such as a dict keyed by name, and returns the original function unchanged, so calls carry no wrapper overhead.
Registration happens when the defining module is imported; a plugin in a module that is never imported is never registered.
A keyed registry decorator such as @register('json') is a decorator factory whose key is captured in a closure.

serves.reason: Building a plugin registry decorator is part of o4's observable product.

requires.reason: Registration is a decoration-time side effect.
Keyed registration uses the factory form.

topics.title: Tagging functions with attributes

kcs.statement: An attribute-tagging decorator sets an attribute on the function object, such as func.deprecated = True, and returns the function so other code can inspect the tag.
If a wrapping decorator without functools.wraps is applied above a tagging decorator, the tag is lost, because wraps is what copies the wrapped function's __dict__.

serves.reason: Attribute tagging is one of the patterns named in o4.

requires.reason: The tag-survival KC depends on wraps copying __dict__.
Determining whether the wrapper receives the tagged function requires bottom-up decorator application.

topics.title: Memoization with functools.lru_cache

kcs.statement: @functools.lru_cache(maxsize=N) stores results keyed by the call's arguments and returns the stored result on repeat calls; maxsize=None, or functools.cache, makes it unbounded.
lru_cache requires every argument to be hashable; calling a cached function with a list argument raises TypeError.
A cached function's cache_info() reports hits, misses, maxsize and currsize, and cache_clear() empties the cache.

serves.reason: Caching is one of the patterns named in o4.

requires.reason: Applying lru_cache uses the @ desugaring.

topics.title: Class decorators: @dec above class

kcs.statement: @dec above class C: ... is equivalent to C = dec(C) applied after the class body has executed; the decorator expression itself is evaluated before the class body runs, and stacked class decorators apply bottom-up.
A class decorator usually modifies the class in place, for example adding a method with setattr, and returns the same class so isinstance and subclassing keep working.

serves.reason: o4 asks for a class decorator that adds a method.
o1 includes desugaring decorated classes.

requires.reason: Class decoration uses the same desugaring as functions.

topics.title: Replacing a class: the singleton decorator

kcs.statement: PEP 318's singleton decorator replaces a class with a function that creates one instance on the first call and returns that same instance on every later call.
Because the singleton decorator rebinds the class name to a function, isinstance(x, Name) raises TypeError and the class can no longer be subclassed by name.

topics.title: What a descriptor is: __get__ on a class attribute

kcs.statement: A descriptor is any object whose type defines __get__, __set__ or __delete__.
__get__(self, obj, objtype) receives the instance as obj, or None when the attribute is looked up on the class itself.
Descriptors take effect only as class attributes; a descriptor stored in an instance's __dict__ is returned as a plain object and its __get__ is not called.

serves.reason: Predicting obj.attr for a descriptor starts from what __get__ receives.

topics.title: Data vs non-data descriptors and lookup order

kcs.statement: A data descriptor defines __set__ or __delete__; a non-data descriptor defines only __get__.

Under default instance lookup, a data descriptor defining __get__ takes precedence over the instance dictionary, which in turn takes precedence over non-data descriptors and plain class attributes; a descriptor without __get__ does not override an instance value on reads.

Under default assignment, a descriptor on the type that defines __set__ handles obj.x = v; a data descriptor defining only __delete__ rejects assignment with AttributeError; otherwise v is stored in the instance dictionary when one is available, shadowing any non-data descriptor.
__getattr__ is called only after normal lookup, including descriptors and the instance dictionary, raises AttributeError.

serves.reason: Predicting obj.attr requires the lookup precedence rules.

requires.reason: Precedence is defined over descriptors and __get__.

topics.title: __set_name__: descriptors that know their name

kcs.statement: When a class is created, type.__new__ calls __set_name__(self, owner, name) on each class attribute that defines it, passing the attribute's name.
A descriptor should store per-instance values on the instance, for example under a private name derived in __set_name__; storing them on the descriptor itself shares one value across all instances.

topics.title: @property as a data descriptor

kcs.statement: property(fget, fset, fdel, doc) creates a data descriptor, and @property on a method is the same as property(method).
@x.setter returns a new property that copies fget and adds fset, so the setter method must reuse the name x.
Assigning to a property that has no setter raises AttributeError, because the data descriptor takes precedence over the instance __dict__.

serves.reason: o5 asks to explain @property via the descriptor protocol.

topics.title: Functions as descriptors: bound methods

kcs.statement: Functions are non-data descriptors: looking up a function through an instance calls its __get__, which returns a bound method whose __self__ is the instance.
Calling obj.m(a) is equivalent to type(obj).m(obj, a); the bound method inserts the instance as the first argument.

A decorator implemented as a class with __call__ but no __get__ breaks when applied to a method, because its instances do not bind and self is not passed; a closure-based wrapper is a function and binds normally.

serves.reason: Decorating methods correctly depends on how functions bind.

requires.reason: Binding is the non-data descriptor case of the protocol.

topics.title: @classmethod and @staticmethod under the hood

kcs.statement: staticmethod's __get__ returns the underlying function unchanged, so neither the instance nor the class is passed.
classmethod's __get__ binds the function to the class (type(obj) when accessed through an instance), so cls is passed as the first argument.
A classmethod called on a subclass receives the subclass as cls, which makes it the right tool for alternative constructors that return cls(...).

When combined with a custom function decorator, @classmethod or @staticmethod should be the outermost (top) decorator; a custom wrapper placed above it yields a plain function that binds as an ordinary instance method.

serves.reason: o5 asks to explain classmethod and staticmethod via descriptors and decorate methods correctly.

requires.reason: Both are defined by how they change binding.
The ordering KC is about stacking with a custom decorator.

topics.title: Reusable validators built from descriptors

kcs.statement: The Descriptor HowTo's Validator base class is a data descriptor whose __set__ calls an abstract validate(value) before storing, so subclasses only implement validate.
Because validation runs in __set__, assignments in __init__ and every later assignment are checked, and an invalid value raises before anything is stored.
One validator class, such as Number(minvalue=0), can guard many attributes across classes because each descriptor instance gets its own name from __set_name__.

serves.reason: Writing a reusable validator descriptor is o5's observable product.

requires.reason: Per-attribute storage comes from __set_name__.
